opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to the fact that once a model is acting in an external environment, it's no longer just producing a single answer that gets judged in isolation. It's taking a sequence of actions, and each one changes the state of the world it then has to reason about. So small errors compound. If you misread a tool output or make a slightly wrong assumption early on, you can end up ten steps down a path that doesn't make sense, and the model has to notice that and recover, which is something these systems historically haven't been great at.

The second piece is partial observability. In a chat setting, basically everything the model needs is right there in the context. In an environment, whether that's a codebase, a browser, or some company's internal systems, the model has to figure out what it doesn't know and go get it. Knowing when to explore versus when to commit is a real skill, and it's surprisingly hard to teach, because the right amount of information gathering depends so much on the task.

Then there's the messiness of the environments themselves. Real software has flaky tests, ambiguous documentation, APIs that behave a little differently from what they claim. Humans deal with that through a lot of tacit knowledge and judgment, things like "this error is probably transient, let me just retry," and models have to pick up that kind of intuition somewhere.

And finally, from a training perspective, feedback is sparse and delayed. You might only find out whether a long trajectory worked at the very end, and attributing success or failure back to the specific decisions that mattered is genuinely difficult. So a lot of the progress, I think, comes from getting better at building environments and reward signals that actually reflect what we want, not just from scaling the model itself.

r001.rationale: The response mentions flaky tests and unpredictable API behavior, but does not identify uncertainty in the outcomes of experiments performed in an external environment as a source of difficulty.

r002.rationale: It discusses messy real environments but does not say that tasks are harder when those environments are less amenable to simulation.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify waiting on physical-world processes as a source of difficulty.

r004.rationale: It links multi-step interaction to difficulty, noting that actions change the environment's state, errors compound, and a model may end up ten steps down an unproductive path.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way I'd put it is that when a model is just answering a question, the whole problem is sitting right there in front of it. Everything it needs is in the context, and the model's job is basically to think hard and produce a good answer. The moment you put the model in an environment, that stops being true. Now there's state in the world that the model can't see unless it goes and looks, and its actions actually change that state. So the difficulty shifts from "can you reason well" to "can you figure out what you don't know, go get it, and keep track of it over time."

And I think there are a few things that make that genuinely hard. One is that the feedback is sparse and delayed. If you're writing code or operating a browser, you might take twenty or thirty actions before you find out whether any of them were right. The model has to maintain a kind of running hypothesis about what's going on and be willing to revise it when it gets evidence that it was wrong. That's a very different skill from one-shot reasoning, and it's one where the failure modes are kind of insidious. The model doesn't crash, it just confidently continues down a path that stopped making sense ten steps ago.

The second thing is that environments are messy in ways that are hard to anticipate. A tool returns something slightly malformed, a file isn't where the docs say it is, a command times out. Humans are really good at the "huh, that's weird" reflex, where something doesn't match your expectation and you stop and investigate rather than plowing ahead. Getting models to have that reflex, and to have it calibrated so they're not paranoid about everything, is a big part of what we've been working on.

And then the third piece, which I think is underrated, is that training for this is just harder. For a static question, you can collect the answer once and reuse it forever. For an environment, every training episode is the model actually interacting with something, so the data is expensive, it's slow, and the environment itself has to be robust enough that the model doesn't learn to exploit some quirk of it instead of learning the real skill. A lot of what looks like "the model is bad at agentic tasks" is really "we haven't built good enough environments to teach it yet." So I'd say the hard part is partly about the model's capabilities, but a lot of it is about the infrastructure for actually letting the model practice.

r001.rationale: It says an agent may take many actions before learning whether they were right, identifying uncertainty about action outcomes in an environment as a difficulty.

r002.rationale: It discusses the need for robust training environments and the risk of exploiting quirks, but does not say that environments are harder when they are less amenable to simulation.

r003.rationale: It mentions delayed feedback, slow training episodes, and command timeouts, but does not identify waiting on physical-world processes as a difficulty.

r004.rationale: It mentions taking many actions, but does not identify the extent of required interaction with the environment as a dimension of task difficulty.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is that the model has to act without having all the information it needs up front. If you’re answering a question, you can often treat the prompt as the whole problem. But if you’re using a browser or working in a codebase, you have to discover the problem as you go. You take an action, observe what happens, and update your understanding.

That introduces a few different challenges. You have to figure out which actions will actually make progress, but also which actions will give you useful information. You have to keep track of what you’ve tried. And you have to recognize when your assumptions were wrong and recover, rather than continuing down a path just because it was your initial plan.

The other piece is that errors compound. Being pretty reliable on any individual step doesn’t necessarily make you reliable over a long sequence of steps. So I think the interesting question is less, can the model produce a plausible next action, and more, can it use feedback from the environment to keep itself on track all the way to a verifiable result?

r001.rationale: The response describes acting with incomplete information, observing what happens after each action, and correcting wrong assumptions, identifying uncertain environment feedback as a source of difficulty.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss how the environment’s amenability to simulation affects task difficulty.

r003.rationale: It does not mention waiting on physical-world processes.

r004.rationale: It says errors compound over a long sequence of steps, linking the amount of interaction required to reliability and difficulty.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is that you don’t get to see the whole problem up front. You take an action, the environment changes, and you get some observation back. Then you have to figure out: Did that do what I expected? What did I learn? Should I keep going with this plan, or change it?

So the difficulty isn’t just choosing one good action. It’s maintaining a useful understanding of what’s happening over a sequence of actions, often with incomplete information and feedback that’s delayed or ambiguous. If something goes wrong ten steps in, you might not know which earlier decision caused it.

And that makes recovery really important. A model can have a lot of knowledge and still struggle if it doesn’t recognize that its last action failed, or if it keeps repeating an approach that isn’t working. In an external environment, being able to check your progress and revise your approach is part of solving the task.

r001.rationale: It describes uncertainty about whether an action had the expected effect and says feedback can be incomplete or ambiguous, identifying uncertain outcomes as a difficulty.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss whether the environment is amenable to simulation.

r003.rationale: It mentions delayed feedback, but not unavoidable waiting for physical-world processes.

r004.rationale: It describes reasoning across a sequence of actions, but does not identify the extent of required interaction as a dimension of task difficulty.
